newsitem.title: CHINA: Tung stamps authority on new Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Tung stamps authority on new Hong Kong.

text.p: - Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa stamped his authority on China's rich new region on Wednesday as euphoria faded after all the handover parties.

Tung, handpicked by Beijing to run Hong Kong, won backing for his drive to beat rocketing property prices and he took over the old British governor's residence to hand out honours to the backers of China.
China's stock markets were hit by a handover hangover just two days after Britain gave Hong Kong back to Beijing. Shares fell sharply in Shanghai and Shenzhen.
But China showed no sign of slowing the pace on the political front, urging Taiwan to follow in Hong Kong's footsteps and reunite with the mainland.
"The prospect of complete national reunification... now stands promisingly in sight," Chinese President Jiang Zemin told a jubilant Beijing rally on Tuesday night.
Chinese leaders see Hong Kong -- returned to Beijing under a "one country, two systems" formula -- as a model for Taiwan. But Taiwan is deeply distrustful of honeyed words from Beijing.
For five decades, it has resisted Chairman Mao Zedong's bombast and bombs and successor Deng Xiaoping's promise of lucrative chunks of the mainland's "socialist market economy".

Hong Kong's market reopens on Thursday with financiers keenly watching to see if the Hang Seng Index can rise to new heights after one of the world's richest and most free economies was handed over to the world's last communist monolith.
Dealers are confident the Hong Kong dollar will take the new regime in its stride.
"The foreign currency reserves of the Hong Kong authority are so massive, they would crush any sort of speculative attack on the currency," said one London currency analyst.

Hong Kong and Chinese officials are keen to maintain the currency's stability and stress the continuation of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and the independence of Hong Kong's monetary system from China.
Hong Kong, enjoying a five-day holiday, was lashed by heavy rain and thunderstorms but the shopping malls and restaurants were still packed with crowds in carnival mood.

Tung won a mixed reception for his ambitious policy blueprint for Hong Kong's 6.4 million people. He pledged in his inaugural address to curb property speculators, boost land reclamation and improve education.
Editorial reaction was cautious with the English-language South China Morning Post saying: "He has an inspiring vision for the SAR (Special Administrative Region), but some goals may be elusive."

"The 'one country, two systems' concept is encouraging, but there is still a long and harsh way to put it into reality," Ming Pao Daily News said. "There is no need for either pessimism or praise-singing."

A poll published in the Ming Pao newspaper showed 56 percent of the people backing his moves to curb property speculation. He has promised to increase land supply and plans a 70 percent home ownership rate in a decade.
Just three days after Britain's Prince Charles knighted loyal colonial servants in the chandeliered ballroom of Government House, Tung was there to hand out his own awards for services to China.

In a ceremony rich in irony, one of the Grand Bauhinia awards went to Henry Fok Ying-tung, a business and real estate tycoon cold-shouldered for decades by the British as a communist sympathiser with mainland China.
Fok broke the U.N. embargo on China during the Korean War and helped broker Chinese participation in a bail-out of Tung's family shipping company in the 1980s.
